lesson.title: ATP Hydrolysis: Cashing In the Phosphate Bond
lesson.summary: ATP hydrolysis is the exergonic reaction in which water splits off the terminal phosphate of ATP to form ADP and inorganic phosphate, releasing free energy that the cell can capture and redirect to do work.
lesson.body:
ATP hydrolysis is a water mediated reaction in which a molecule of water attacks the terminal, or gamma, phosphate group of ATP, breaking the phosphoanhydride bond that holds it on and producing adenosine diphosphate, ADP, plus free inorganic phosphate, written Pi. The overall reaction is ATP plus water yields ADP plus Pi. Under standard biochemical conditions this reaction releases roughly seven point three kilocalories, about thirty kilojoules, per mole, and inside an actual living cell the value is typically even larger in magnitude, often cited in the range of eleven to thirteen kilocalories per mole, because cellular concentrations of ATP, ADP, and Pi are held far from the equilibrium point used to define the standard value.

Why does breaking that one bond release so much usable energy? Part of the answer sits in the structure covered in the previous chapter: the three phosphate groups of ATP are all negatively charged and forced close together, so removing one relieves a substantial amount of electrostatic repulsion among the remaining charges. The other part of the answer is that the direct products, ADP and free phosphate, are more stable than the reactant, partly because the released phosphate ion can spread its negative charge across multiple oxygen atoms through resonance in a way that is more restricted while it is still locked into the triphosphate chain. Put together, the products sit at meaningfully lower free energy than ATP and water did, which is exactly the definition of an exergonic reaction: delta G is negative, and free energy is released rather than absorbed.

This is why ATP hydrolysis is the textbook example paired against endergonic reactions rather than treated as some separate, unrelated phenomenon. Every endergonic step in the cell needs an energy donor with a sufficiently negative delta G, and ATP hydrolysis reliably supplies one. In cells this reaction essentially never happens as an uncontrolled dump of heat into solution; instead it is catalyzed by specific enzymes broadly called ATPases, which harness the released energy for a purpose, such as changing the shape of a motor protein, pumping an ion across a membrane, or transferring the phosphate group itself onto another molecule.

A related and biologically important variant is hydrolysis at the other phosphoanhydride bond, splitting ATP into AMP and pyrophosphate, PPi, a linked pair of phosphate groups, rather than into ADP and a single phosphate. This route is used, for example, when amino acids are activated for protein synthesis by aminoacyl tRNA synthetases, and during nucleic acid synthesis by DNA and RNA polymerases. A second enzyme, inorganic pyrophosphatase, then rapidly hydrolyzes the released pyrophosphate into two separate phosphate ions. That second hydrolysis is itself strongly exergonic and effectively irreversible, and it pulls the entire multistep process forward by removing a product, a clean example of how ATP breakdown can make reactions run reliably in one direction.

The bottom line connects three ideas already introduced: ATP's structure, the concept of Gibbs free energy, and the category of exergonic reactions. ATP hydrolysis is exergonic precisely because of how ATP is built, and its negative delta G is what gives the cell a dependable, on demand packet of free energy. That packet does not usually escape as wasted heat. Instead, as the next chapter explains, cells almost always spend it by coupling ATP hydrolysis directly to a reaction that would otherwise never happen on its own.
